title: Rectifiers, PFC & Inverters
description: Power factor and harmonics of rectifiers, the boost PFC rectifier, and single- and three-phase PWM inverters for AC loads and motor drives.

study.title: Power factor with distorted currents
study.body: Power factor is real power over apparent power, $PF = P/(V_{rms}I_{rms})$. With a sinusoidal voltage only the fundamental current carries real power, so $PF$ splits into a **displacement factor** $\cos\varphi_1$ and a **distortion factor** $I_{1,rms}/I_{rms} = 1/\sqrt{1 + THD^2}$, where the total harmonic distortion is $THD = \sqrt{\sum_{n\ge2}I_n^2}/I_1$. Harmonic currents raise $I_{rms}$, losses and the required wiring, without delivering power.

study.title: The capacitor-input rectifier
study.body: A diode bridge feeding a large capacitor only conducts near the voltage peaks, when the line exceeds the capacitor voltage. The current flows in short, tall pulses, rich in odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th, …): $THD$ is often above 100 % and $PF$ only 0.5–0.7, even though the pulses are centred on the voltage peaks. Standards such as IEC 61000-3-2 limit these harmonics for most equipment above 75 W.

study.title: The ideal rectifier and boost PFC
study.body: An ideal rectifier behaves like a resistor $R_e$ on the line: $i_g = v_g/R_e$, so $PF$ = 1. A **boost PFC** converter after the diode bridge achieves this: its controller shapes the inductor (= line) current to follow the rectified voltage, and adjusts $R_e$ to deliver the required power. The duty cycle varies over each half-cycle as $d = 1 - |v_g|/V$, so the output $V$ must exceed the line peak.

study.title: Twice-line ripple and hold-up
study.body: With a resistor-like input, the input power $p(t) = P(1 - \cos 2\omega t)$ pulsates at twice the line frequency, while the load draws a constant $P$. The output capacitor buffers the difference, so $V$ has a ripple at 100 Hz (50 Hz mains). The same capacitor also provides **hold-up**: it keeps the downstream converter running for a time $t_h$ after the mains drops out, while $V$ sags to the minimum the next stage accepts.

study.title: The H-bridge inverter
study.body: Two half-bridge legs make an inverter: $Q_1$/$Q_4$ on gives $v_{ab} = +V_{dc}$, $Q_2$/$Q_3$ gives $-V_{dc}$, and both upper (or both lower) switches give 0. Switches in one leg must never conduct together (**shoot-through**), so a short dead time separates them. A square-wave drive gives a fundamental of amplitude $\frac{4}{\pi}V_{dc}$ but large low-order harmonics; PWM moves the harmonics up to the switching frequency where the load inductance filters them.

study.title: Explore: sinusoidal PWM
study.body: Each leg compares a sinusoidal reference with a triangular carrier at $f_s$; the **modulation index** $m_a$ is the ratio of their amplitudes. The local average of $v_{ab}$ follows $m_aV_{dc}\sin\omega t$, linearly up to $m_a$ = 1. The frequency ratio $m_f = f_s/f_1$ (here 9) sets where the harmonics are. Drag $m_a$ (bipolar PWM shown).

study.title: Three-phase inverters and motor drives
study.body: Three legs, with references 120° apart, drive a three-phase load. Each leg's average is $\frac{V_{dc}}{2}(1 + m_a\sin\cdot)$, so the line-to-line fundamental has rms value $\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sqrt2}m_aV_{dc} \approx 0.612\,m_aV_{dc}$. Adding a third harmonic to the references (it cancels between lines) stretches the linear range to $m_a$ = 1.155. Six-step (square-wave) operation gives $\frac{\sqrt6}{\pi}V_{dc} \approx 0.78\,V_{dc}$. An induction-motor drive keeps $V/f$ constant below rated speed so that the flux stays constant.

study.title: Worked example: boost PFC
study.body:
230 V, 50 Hz mains, $P$ = 500 W, $V$ = 400 V, $C$ = 330 µF.
- $R_e = V_{rms}^2/P$ = 230²/500 = 105.8 Ω; $I_{rms}$ = 2.17 A, peak 3.07 A.
- Line peak 325 V, so $d$ at the peak = 1 − 325/400 = 0.19; near the zero crossings $d \to 1$.
- 100 Hz ripple: $P/(2\pi \cdot 50 \cdot CV)$ = 500/(2π × 50 × 330 µF × 400 V) = 12.1 V peak-to-peak.

steps.title: Two reasons for a low power factor
steps.body: $PF = P/(V_{rms}I_{rms})$. A phase shift between the fundamental current and the voltage lowers it (displacement factor $\cos\varphi_1$), and so do harmonics, which add rms current but no power (distortion factor $I_1/I_{rms}$).

steps.prompt: A single-phase load draws {{P|W}} from {{V}} V rms mains with an rms current of {{I|A}}. What is its power factor?
A rectifier's input current contains (rms values) a fundamental of {{I1|A}}, a 3rd harmonic of {{I3|A}}, a 5th of {{I5|A}} and a 7th of {{I7|A}}; higher harmonics are negligible. Find the $THD$ in %.
A load's current has a $THD$ of {{thd}} % and its fundamental lags the voltage by {{phi}}°. What is the power factor?
steps.explanation: Distortion factor: $1/\sqrt{1 + THD^2}$ = 1/√(1 + {{thd/100}}²) = {{1/sqrt(1+(thd/100)^2)||3}}. Displacement factor: cos {{phi}}° = {{cos(rad(phi))||3}}. $PF$ = **{{cos(rad(phi))/sqrt(1+(thd/100)^2)||3}}**.

steps.title: Why diode rectifiers are bad loads
steps.body: A diode bridge with a large reservoir capacitor only conducts for a short time around each voltage peak. The current pulses are in phase with the voltage (displacement factor ≈ 1) but very distorted, so the power factor is poor.

steps.prompt: Which of these loads typically has the **lowest** power factor?
options: A diode bridge feeding a large capacitor (no PFC)
An induction motor at full load
A power supply with an active boost PFC stage
steps.explanation: The heater has $PF$ = 1, a loaded induction motor about 0.8–0.9 (displacement only) and a boost-PFC supply above 0.95. The capacitor-input rectifier's narrow current pulses give $PF$ ≈ 0.5–0.7.

steps.prompt: A large DC-side inductor makes a rectifier draw a square-wave line current of ±{{I|A}}, in phase with the voltage.

ask.prompt: What is the rms value of its fundamental?
ask.explanation: The fundamental of a square wave of height $I$ has peak $\frac{4}{\pi}I$, so rms $\frac{2\sqrt2}{\pi}I$ = 0.900 × {{I|A}} = **{{2*sqrt(2)/pi*I|A}}**. The total rms is $I$ itself, so $PF$ = 0.90.

steps.prompt: A diode rectifier whose current pulses are centred on the voltage peaks has a power factor of 1, because its current is in phase with the voltage.
steps.explanation: Being in phase only makes the **displacement** factor ≈ 1. The pulses contain large harmonics, which add rms current but carry no power, so the distortion factor (and thus $PF$) is well below 1.

steps.title: Emulating a resistor
steps.body: A boost converter after the diode bridge draws its inductor current straight from the rectified line. The controller makes that current proportional to the rectified voltage, $i_g = v_g/R_e$, so the line sees a resistor: $PF$ = 1. A slow outer loop adjusts $R_e$ to keep $V$ at its setpoint.

steps.prompt: A boost PFC stage draws {{P|W}} from {{V}} V rms mains with $PF$ = 1.

ask.prompt: What emulated resistance $R_e$ does the line see?
What is the peak line current?
ask.explanation: $I_{rms} = P/V_{rms}$ = {{P/V|A}}, and the current is sinusoidal, so $I_{pk} = \sqrt2 I_{rms}$ = **{{sqrt(2)*P/V|A}}**.

steps.prompt: A boost PFC converter on {{V}} V rms mains makes $V$ = {{Vo|V}}.

ask.prompt: What is its duty cycle at the peak of the line voltage?
What is its duty cycle 30° after a zero crossing?

steps.prompt: A boost PFC runs from a line with a {{Vpk|V}} peak. The graph shows its duty cycle over one half line cycle. Set the output voltage $V$ so that the smallest duty cycle is {{dmin}}.
steps.explanation: The smallest duty cycle occurs at the line peak: $d_{min} = 1 - V_{pk}/V$ → $V = \frac{V_{pk}}{1 - d_{min}}$ = {{Vpk}} / {{1-dmin||2}} = **{{Vpk/(1-dmin)|V}}**. A higher $V$ gives more control margin but more switch voltage and switching loss.

steps.title: Energy buffering
steps.body: The line delivers $p(t) = P(1 - \cos 2\omega t)$, the load wants a constant $P$. The output capacitor absorbs the difference, so $V$ ripples at twice the line frequency. The PFC voltage loop must be slow (≈10–20 Hz) so it does not try to remove this ripple and distort the input current.

steps.prompt: A {{P|W}} PFC stage on {{f}} Hz mains has $V$ = {{Vo|V}} and $C$ = {{C|F}}. Estimate the peak-to-peak output ripple.
A {{P|W}} supply must keep running for {{th|s}} after a mains dropout. Its PFC bus is at {{Vo|V}} and the DC–DC stage works down to {{Vmin|V}}. What is the minimum bus capacitance?
Why is the boost the usual topology for single-phase PFC?
options: Its inductor sits in series with the input, so the line current is continuous and directly controllable
It steps the voltage down, which suits the low line voltage
steps.explanation: In a boost the input current equals the inductor current, which the controller can shape cycle by cycle into a smooth half-sine. A buck's input current is pulsed and it cannot operate when $v_g < V$. Isolation, if needed, comes from the following DC–DC stage.

steps.prompt: The output voltage of a boost PFC stage must be higher than the peak of the line voltage.
steps.explanation: A boost can only step up: $V = |v_g|/(1-d) \ge |v_g|$. If $V$ were below the line peak, the diodes would conduct uncontrolled near the peaks. Typically $V \approx$ 380–400 V for universal (85–265 V) mains.

steps.title: From DC to AC
steps.body: An H-bridge connects the load to $+V_{dc}$, $-V_{dc}$ or 0. Driven with a 50 % square wave it produces a fundamental of peak $\frac{4}{\pi}V_{dc}$, plus 3rd, 5th, 7th… harmonics that are hard to filter. PWM fixes that by switching much faster than the output frequency.

steps.prompt: An H-bridge inverter on a {{Vdc|V}} DC bus is driven with a square wave (no PWM). What is the rms value of the fundamental output voltage?

steps.title: Sinusoidal PWM
steps.body: Comparing a sine reference with a fast triangular carrier makes each leg's local duty cycle follow the sine. The average of $v_{ab}$ is then $m_aV_{dc}\sin\omega t$: its amplitude is set by the modulation index $m_a$, its frequency by the reference. Drag $m_a$.

steps.prompt: A full-bridge inverter with sinusoidal PWM runs from {{Vdc|V}} at $m_a$ = {{m}}. What is the rms value of the fundamental output voltage?
A full-bridge PWM inverter runs from {{Vdc|V}}. Set the modulation index for an output fundamental of {{Vt|V}} rms.
A **half-bridge** inverter (one leg, load to the midpoint of a split {{Vdc|V}} bus) uses sinusoidal PWM with $m_a$ = {{m}}. What is the peak of the fundamental output voltage?
steps.explanation: The leg output swings between $\pm V_{dc}/2$ around the midpoint, so $\hat v_1 = \frac12m_aV_{dc}$ = 0.5 × {{m}} × {{Vdc}} = **{{0.5*m*Vdc|V}}**, half of what a full bridge gives from the same bus.

steps.prompt: An inverter makes {{f1}} Hz using a {{fs|Hz}} triangular carrier.

ask.prompt: What is the frequency modulation ratio $m_f$?
ask.explanation: $m_f = f_s/f_1$ = {{fs|Hz}} / {{f1}} Hz = **{{fs/f1||4}}**. With bipolar PWM the main harmonics cluster around $m_f f_1 = f_s$ and its multiples.

ask.prompt: With unipolar PWM, the first harmonic cluster sits around twice the carrier frequency. At what frequency is that?
ask.explanation: In unipolar PWM the two legs switch at different instants, so the output pulses occur at twice the carrier rate: harmonics cluster around $2f_s$ = **{{2*fs|Hz}}**, easier to filter.

steps.prompt: Match each H-bridge switch state to the result (Q_1, Q_2: left leg top/bottom; Q_3, Q_4: right leg top/bottom)
steps.explanation: Node a is at $V_{dc}$ when $Q_1$ is on and at 0 when $Q_2$ is on; node b likewise with $Q_3$/$Q_4$. Turning on both switches of one leg shorts the DC bus, which is why drivers insert a dead time between them.

steps.prompt: A three-phase inverter with sinusoidal PWM runs from {{Vdc|V}} at $m_a$ = {{m}}.

ask.prompt: What is the rms line-to-line output voltage (fundamental)?
What is the rms line-to-neutral voltage (fundamental) of a balanced star load?

steps.prompt: A drive must supply a {{VLL}} V (line-to-line rms) motor with linear sinusoidal PWM.

ask.prompt: What minimum DC bus voltage is needed at $m_a$ = 1?
With third-harmonic injection ($m_a$ up to 1.155), what minimum bus voltage is needed?

steps.prompt: An induction motor is rated {{Vr}} V at 50 Hz and has {{p}} poles. A V/f drive runs it at {{f}} Hz.

ask.prompt: What voltage should the drive apply (constant V/f)?
ask.explanation: $V = V_{rated}\frac{f}{f_{rated}}$ = {{Vr}} V × {{f}}/50 = **{{Vr*f/50|V}}**. This keeps the air-gap flux, and so the available torque, constant.

ask.prompt: What is the synchronous speed in rpm?
ask.explanation: $n_s = \frac{120f}{p}$ = 120 × {{f}} / {{p}} = **{{120*f/p}} rpm**. The rotor runs slightly slower (slip).

steps.prompt: A drive's DC bus comes from a three-phase diode bridge on {{VLL}} V (line-to-line rms) mains, giving $V_{dc} \approx 1.35\,V_{LL}$. With linear SPWM ($m_a \le 1$), what is the highest line-to-line rms voltage the inverter can deliver?
steps.explanation: $V_{dc}$ ≈ 1.35 × {{VLL}} = {{1.35*VLL|V}}. Maximum: $0.612\,V_{dc}$ = **{{1.35*VLL*sqrt(3)/(2*sqrt(2))|V}}**, only about 83 % of the mains voltage. That is why drives use third-harmonic injection, space-vector PWM or overmodulation to reach rated voltage.

steps.prompt: A three-phase inverter on a {{Vdc|V}} bus is run in six-step (square-wave) mode. What is the rms value of the fundamental line-to-line voltage?
steps.explanation: Each leg is a ±$V_{dc}/2$ square wave with fundamental peak $\frac{4}{\pi}\frac{V_{dc}}{2}$; line-to-line multiplies by √3, and rms divides by √2: $\frac{\sqrt6}{\pi}V_{dc}$ = **{{sqrt(6)/pi*Vdc|V}}**. That beats linear SPWM ({{sqrt(3)/(2*sqrt(2))*Vdc|V}} at $m_a$ = 1) and third-harmonic PWM ({{Vdc/sqrt(2)|V}}), at the price of low-order harmonics.

steps.prompt: In a three-phase inverter, adding the same third harmonic to all three leg references changes the phase-leg voltages but not the line-to-line voltages.
steps.explanation: The third harmonic is identical (in phase) in all three legs, because 3 × 120° = 360°. Line-to-line voltages are differences of leg voltages, so it cancels. It lowers the peak of each leg's reference, which allows $m_a$ up to 1.155 without overmodulating.

steps.prompt: A mains-powered chain: a boost PFC ({{e1*100}} %), a DC–DC stage ({{e2*100}} %) and an inverter ({{e3*100}} %) in cascade deliver {{Po|W}}. How much power is drawn from the grid?
steps.explanation: Efficiencies multiply: $\eta$ = {{e1}} × {{e2}} × {{e3}} = {{e1*e2*e3||3}}. $P_{in} = P_{out}/\eta$ = {{Po|W}} / {{e1*e2*e3||3}} = **{{Po/(e1*e2*e3)|W}}**, of which {{Po/(e1*e2*e3)-Po|W}} becomes heat.
